titleText.es: Necesitamos un día de fiesta especial para honrar a las incontables buenas almas con redes inseguras de nombre 'linksys'.
titleText.en: We need a special holiday to honor the countless kind souls with unsecured networks named 'linksys'.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official title text, using buenas almas for “kind souls” and de nombre for “named.”

regions.labelEs: HAY POCAS FUERZAS MÁS PODEROSAS QUE UN GEEK INTENTANDO DESESPERADAMENTE PILLAR INTERNET EN UN PISO NUEVO.

applications.explanationEn: Más raises the degree of poderosas, and que opens the comparison.
Poderosas uses feminine plural -as because it describes the feminine plural noun fuerzas.
Intentando supplies the changing form of intentar, while pillar remains in its unchanged -ar form as the attempted action.
Desesperada takes -mente to form the word that describes how the attempt is made.
Piso names the home first, and nuevo follows as its neutral description.
Nuevo uses masculine singular -o because it describes the masculine singular noun piso.

regions.labelEs: VALE, LA ANTENA DE PRINGLES NOS DEJA CONECTARNOS A LA WIFI DEL OTRO LADO DE LA CALLE.

excludedUnits.rationale: Pringles is the unchanged commercial brand name printed on the improvised antenna reference, not Spanish vocabulary; the linked concept preserves its role in the joke.

applications.explanationEn: Nos identifies the people who receive permission, deja supplies the allowing action, and conectarnos gives the action they are allowed to perform.
Nos is attached to the unchanged action conectar and refers to the people getting themselves connected.
Conectarnos carries the matching nos, a introduces the network being joined, and la wifi names that network.

applications.exampleEs: DEL OTRO LADO DE LA CALLE
applications.explanationEn: Del combines de and el before otro lado, and de la calle names the place whose opposite side is meant.
The ordinary form tienen stays in place; the question marks and intonation turn the idea into a yes-or-no question without an extra helper word.

regions.labelEs: NO, PERO CREO QUE EL TÉCNICO DEL CABLE VA A CONECTARLES ANTES A ELLOS.

applications.explanationEn: Va matches the one technician, a links to the planned action, and conectar remains unchanged inside conectarles.
Les is attached to the unchanged action conectar and identifies several people receiving the connection.
Les inside conectarles marks the plural recipients, while a ellos names those same people explicitly; antes states that they will receive the service first.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is more of a certain quality than another?
cards.answerEn: Put más before the describing word and que before the other thing.
cards.noteEn: The describing word is an adjective, such as alto for “tall” or importante for “important.” Más raises the degree, and que introduces what you compare it with.

example.es: Este libro es más corto que aquel.
example.en: This book is shorter than that one.

cards.noteEn: Geek is an English borrowing used informally in Spanish for someone intensely interested in technology or another specialized subject. Friki is another common Spanish option.

example.es: Es un geek de la informática.

cards.noteEn: Intentando is the -ando form of intentar. It presents the attempt as an action in progress or happening alongside another description.

example.en: He keeps trying to open the door.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.noteEn: Desesperadamente describes how an action is done. It is formed from the feminine singular describing form desesperada plus -mente.

example.en: He was desperately looking for the keys.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.answerEn: to get; to pick up (a signal or internet access, informal)
cards.noteEn: Pillar has several informal meanings, especially in Spain. With a signal, coverage, or internet access, it can mean managing to get or pick it up.

example.en: I cannot pick up a signal here.

cards.noteEn: Piso can mean a floor or storey. In Spain it also commonly means an apartment or flat where someone lives.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.
An antena sends or receives radio signals, including television, mobile, and wireless-network signals.

example.es: La antena recibe una señal débil.
example.en: The antenna receives a weak signal.

cards.questionEn: What is the improvised antenna in this comic doing?
cards.answerEn: It is a homemade directional wireless antenna made from a cylindrical snack can to reach a Wi-Fi network farther away.
cards.noteEn: The official English text calls it a “Pringles cantenna.” The joke uses that improvised antenna to reach the network across the street before the characters' own service is connected.

example.es: Una antena direccional concentra la señal.
example.en: A directional antenna concentrates the signal.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets another person do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, mark the person receiving permission with me, te, le, nos, os, or les, and put the allowed action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form is the verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The person marker can stand before a changed form of dejar, join an affirmative command such as déjame, or in some structures join the following dictionary-form verb. Dejar changes for the person and time; the allowed action does not.
Deja is a present form of dejar used with one person or thing that permits an action. A short word such as me, te, nos, or les can identify who is allowed to act.

cards.answerEn: to connect; to get ourselves connected
cards.noteEn: Conectarnos joins the unchanged action conectar to nos. Here nos refers to the people who connect themselves to a network.

example.es: Vamos a conectarnos a la red.
example.en: We are going to connect to the network.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.promptEs: conectarse a Internet / a una red
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone connects to the internet or a network?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of conectarse, then a before Internet, la red, or the service being joined.
cards.noteEn: Conectarse uses me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person connecting. Keep a before the destination: me conecto a la red, te conectas a Internet. In an unchanged verb form, the small pronoun attaches to the end, as in conectarte.

example.es: Nos conectamos a Internet por la mañana.
example.en: We connect to the internet in the morning.

cards.answerEn: to; required before what someone connects to
cards.noteEn: Conectarse normally takes a before the network, service, or device being joined.
Wifi is used as a Spanish noun. It is often feminine because red, 'network,' is understood: la wifi. Usage and pronunciation vary by region.

example.es: La wifi del hotel es lenta.

cards.answerEn: from the (de + el, identifying a source or location)
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. When something comes from a place or side, de can mean “from.”

example.en: I hear music from the other room.

cards.questionEn: How do you identify the opposite side of a place, street, or object?
cards.answerEn: Use el otro lado de, then name the place or object.
cards.noteEn: Al otro lado de often describes where something is; del otro lado de can identify something coming from that opposite side. Al combines a + el, and del combines de + el.

example.es: La farmacia está al otro lado de la plaza.
example.en: The pharmacy is on the other side of the square.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, técnico names a trained worker who installs, maintains, or repairs equipment or a service. La técnica can name a female technician.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; de + el links a worker to a service
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use de after a job title to identify the service or area involved. Del combines de and el; English often places that service directly before the job title.
Cable can name the physical wire, or the television and internet service delivered through a cable network.

example.es: El servicio de cable llega mañana.

cards.answerEn: is going to (before a future action)
cards.noteEn: Va normally means ‘goes.’ Before a and an unchanged action verb, it helps express what one person or thing is going to do.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
to connect them; to hook them up
cards.noteEn: Conectarles joins the unchanged action conectar to les, which identifies several people receiving the connection or service.

example.es: Van a conectarles el teléfono mañana.
example.en: They are going to hook up their telephone tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cards.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, then use a phrase beginning with the word a to identify the receiver explicitly.
cards.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once. In the prompt, the slash means that le and les are alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and the named receiver.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces an emphasized object such as a mí
cards.noteEn: A stressed form such as a mí can repeat a short object pronoun such as me for contrast or emphasis. English normally expresses the emphasis through stress rather than an extra word.

example.en: You cannot see me in particular.

cards.answerEn: them (masculine or mixed group, after a preposition)
cards.noteEn: Ellos usually means ‘they,’ but after a preposition such as con, para, or sin, English uses ‘them.’
